misconceptions.description: The student holds that the sign of acceleration by itself decides whether a particle is speeding up or slowing down, so that negative acceleration is read as slowing down regardless of the direction of travel. The reports name this belief directly as a misconception seen in responses.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for a judgement about speed at an instant where velocity and acceleration are both negative, and require the reason to be stated; a student holding this belief answers slowing down.
misconceptions.name: Speed is governed by acceleration alone

misconceptions.description: The student treats the definite integral of velocity and the definite integral of the absolute value of velocity as the same quantity, so displacement is offered where total distance was asked. The 2023 report describes this as an incomplete understanding of the difference between displacement and total distance travelled.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for both the displacement and the total distance over an interval on which the velocity changes sign; a student holding this belief reports the same number twice.
misconceptions.name: The integral of velocity gives total distance

misconceptions.description: The student selects an integrand by the surface shape of the prompt rather than by the geometry described, squaring a difference of functions for an area, inserting pi where nothing is revolved, or treating a described rectangular cross section as a square. The 2025 report says such integrands suggest misconceptions about constructing an appropriate integral to find an area or a volume.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give one region and ask in turn for its area, for the volume of a solid with a stated non-square cross section, and for the volume on revolution about a line other than an axis; a student holding this belief writes integrands that differ only by a constant.
misconceptions.name: Area and volume integrands are interchangeable

misconceptions.description: The student reads the integral of f prime from a lower limit to x as simply f of x, so the value at the lower limit and the direction of the limits play no role. The 2023 report names this as the most common misconception in applying the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus on that question.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the value of an accumulation function at a point to the left of its lower limit; a student holding this belief reports a positive area and never applies the sign change.
misconceptions.name: An accumulation function equals the integrand's antiderivative outright

misconceptions.description: The student does not distinguish the variable of differentiation, so implicit differentiation with respect to time is carried out with respect to x, and the several notations for derivative and differential are used interchangeably. The reports describe responses that had difficulty understanding differentiation with respect to a variable other than x.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an implicit relation together with a rate with respect to time and ask for the other rate with respect to time; a student holding this belief produces a derivative with respect to x and stops.
misconceptions.name: Derivatives with respect to x and with respect to t are the same object

misconceptions.description: The student treats the two phrases as synonyms, so a difference quotient is offered for an average value, or the derivative is integrated in place of the function. The 2025 report lists finding average rate of change instead of average value among the two most common misconceptions on that part.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for both the average value of a function and its average rate of change on the same interval; a student holding this belief gives one number for both.
misconceptions.name: Average value and average rate of change are the same quantity
misconceptions.official_evidence_notes: 2023 AB/BC Q1(c), cr-23:4; 2025 AB/BC Q1(A), crabbc-25:3 and crabbc-25:4

misconceptions.description: The student equates the value produced by an error bound formula with the actual error of the approximation, writing the error as equal to the bound or as strictly less than it. The 2025 report states that the error is not equal to the bound and the bound is not strictly less than it, and the 2023 report asks for repeated practice communicating the difference between an error and an error bound.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to state what the bound guarantees about the difference between the approximation and the exact value, using an inequality; a student holding this belief writes an equality.
misconceptions.name: An error bound is the error
misconceptions.official_evidence_notes: 2023 BC Q6(b), cr-23:35 and cr-23:36; 2025 BC Q5(C), crabbc-25:33 and crabbc-25:34

misconceptions.description: The student substitutes the infinity symbol for the variable and computes with the result, so limit notation becomes a formality that can be introduced and then dropped. The 2023 report names arithmetic performed with infinity among the errors in evaluating an improper integral, and the scoring notes are cited as calling this out.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for a convergent improper integral and require every line of the evaluation; a student holding this belief writes a reciprocal of infinity rather than a limit.
misconceptions.name: Infinity is a number available for arithmetic

misconceptions.description: The student recalls a theorem by its conclusion and applies it without establishing the conditions, so continuity is asserted rather than derived from differentiability and the required bracketing values are never shown. The 2025 report states that many students attempted to apply the conclusion of the Intermediate Value Theorem without first explicitly checking the required conditions.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Present a function that fails one hypothesis and ask whether the theorem's conclusion follows; a student holding this belief asserts the conclusion anyway.
misconceptions.name: A theorem's conclusion may be used without its hypotheses
misconceptions.official_evidence_notes: 2023 AB/BC Q1(b), cr-23:3 and cr-23:4; 2025 AB/BC Q3(B), crabbc-25:12 and crabbc-25:14

misconceptions.description: The student appears to treat a sign change of the derivative at one point as sufficient to name an absolute extremum on a closed interval, so endpoints and other critical points are never compared. The reports record the behaviour and describe the arguments as local rather than global; the underlying belief is an inference from that pattern.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for an absolute minimum on a closed interval where the only interior sign change gives a local minimum that is not the global one; a student holding this belief names the interior point.
misconceptions.name: A local sign change establishes a global extremum
misconceptions.official_evidence_notes: 2023 AB/BC Q4(d), cr-23:16; 2025 AB/BC Q1(D), crabbc-25:4; 2025 AB/BC Q4(D), crabbc-25:18

misconceptions.description: The student uses the equals sign to join successive lines of work and to attach a calculator value to a symbolic expression, so unequal objects are declared equal. The reports record the behaviour repeatedly and advise teaching the equals sign as a statement of equality rather than punctuation; the belief itself is an inference.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to say which two quantities each equals sign in their own work claims to be equal; a student holding this belief cannot name them for the linking signs.
misconceptions.name: The equals sign is punctuation between steps

misconceptions.description: The student decides whether a linear approximation is an overestimate or an underestimate without consulting the second derivative, treating the two ideas as independent. The 2022 and 2023 reports record responses that did not use given second derivative information; the belief is inferred from that behaviour.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give the sign of the second derivative on an interval and ask, with reasons, whether a tangent line approximation on that interval overestimates or underestimates; a student holding this belief reasons from the direction of the shift instead.
misconceptions.name: Concavity is unrelated to the accuracy of a tangent line approximation

misconceptions.description: The student uses radius of convergence and interval of convergence interchangeably and does not see the endpoints as a separate question. The 2025 report records responses using imprecise language about the radius of convergence rather than the interval of convergence, and the 2024 report notes that students must supply whichever of the two was requested.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the interval of convergence and then, separately, for the radius; a student holding this belief gives the same object for both and omits the endpoint analysis.
misconceptions.name: The radius and the interval of convergence are the same statement
misconceptions.official_evidence_notes: 2024 BC Q6(c), cr-24:36; 2025 BC Q6(A)(D), crabbc-25:37 and crabbc-25:38

misconceptions.description: The student takes numerical values given for one instant as a permanent relationship between the quantities, then uses that relationship to reduce a formula in two changing variables to one variable and avoid the product rule. The reports record the reduction and the assumption that one quantity is constant; the belief is inferred from that behaviour.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a volume formula in two variables with values supplied at one instant and ask for the rate of change of the volume; a student holding this belief substitutes before differentiating.
misconceptions.name: A relation holding at one instant holds identically

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a Riemann sum as an operation on the list of function values alone, so the partition widths play no role and every subinterval is implicitly treated alike.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Present a table whose inputs are unevenly spaced and ask for the value of one term of the sum together with its units.
misconceptions.name: A Riemann sum is a sum of the listed values

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the left, right, and midpoint choices as interchangeable labels rather than as different sample points that give different sums.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the left and the right sum on the same monotone table and ask whether the two values must agree.
misconceptions.name: The endpoint convention is cosmetic

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a Riemann sum as the value of the definite integral rather than as an approximation whose error has a direction.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the reported sum is larger or smaller than the integral and how the student knows.
misconceptions.name: Riemann sums are exact

misconceptions.description: The learner averages across the entire interval rather than forming a separate trapezoid on each subinterval.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the area of the single trapezoid on the first subinterval.
misconceptions.name: A trapezoid is a rectangle at the average height of the whole interval

misconceptions.description: The learner applies one monotonicity rule to every approximation method, so concavity never enters the reasoning.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an increasing concave down rate and ask for the direction of a trapezoidal estimate and of a left sum separately.
misconceptions.name: Approximation direction follows from increase or decrease alone

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate whether a function rises from whether it bends upward, so the two justifications are exchanged freely.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to sketch a decreasing concave up curve.
misconceptions.name: Concavity and monotonicity are the same property

misconceptions.description: The learner attaches every question about the accumulation function to the visible features of the plotted integrand, so extrema and inflection points are read off the wrong curve.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to label the plotted curve and the accumulation function separately before answering.
misconceptions.name: The plotted curve is the function under discussion

misconceptions.description: The learner uses the zeros of f for every feature of g, so both extrema and inflection points are placed at the same inputs.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask where g has extrema and where g has inflection points on the same graph and compare the two lists.
misconceptions.name: A zero of the integrand is a general turning feature of the accumulation function

misconceptions.description: The learner believes that naming the defining property, such as g changing concavity, answers a request for a reason, without connecting the claim to the supplied representation.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what feature of the given graph makes the stated claim true.
misconceptions.name: Restating a definition counts as a reason

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a first or second derivative test at one input as sufficient for an absolute extremum on a closed interval.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the endpoints can beat the interior candidate and how that is checked.
misconceptions.name: A relative extremum test settles an absolute extremum

misconceptions.description: The learner reproduces area formulas for triangles, trapezoids, and semicircles without the halving factor.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the area of a single semicircle of a stated radius.
misconceptions.name: Area formulas are recalled without their fractional factors

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the definite integral as the total area of the region between the graph and the axis, with no sign attached to regions below the axis.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the integral of a rate that is negative on the whole interval.
misconceptions.name: The definite integral measures unsigned area

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the accumulated change as the value of the quantity itself, so the initial condition has no role.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a rate and two different initial values and ask for the value at the later input in each case.
misconceptions.name: The integral of a rate is the amount of the quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate the integral from the integral divided by the interval length, so the two expressions are described and computed interchangeably.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Show both expressions side by side and ask for the units of each.
misconceptions.name: Average value and accumulated amount are the same quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner applies a difference quotient wherever the word average appears, so an average value request is answered with a slope.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the two answers has the units of the function and which has the units of a rate.
misconceptions.name: Average of a function and average rate of change are the same quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner treats u as a shorthand label rather than a change of variable, so limits of integration and differentials carry over unchanged.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the lower limit becomes after the substitution and why.
misconceptions.name: Substitution renames a variable without changing the problem

misconceptions.description: The learner selects substitution from the presence of an inner function alone, without checking that its derivative is present.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write du and point to it inside the integrand.
misconceptions.name: A composite integrand guarantees that substitution applies

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the antiderivative as unique, so the arbitrary constant is decoration rather than part of the answer.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to name two different functions with the same given derivative.
misconceptions.name: An antiderivative is a single function

misconceptions.description: The learner extends the sum rule to products, so each factor is antidifferentiated on its own.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to differentiate the proposed product and compare with the integrand.
misconceptions.name: Antidifferentiation distributes across a product

misconceptions.description: The learner treats infinity as an endpoint value rather than as a limiting process, so improper integrals are evaluated by substitution.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write the improper integral as a limit before antidifferentiating.
misconceptions.name: Infinity is a number that can be substituted

misconceptions.description: The learner concludes convergence from the integrand approaching zero, so the limit is never examined.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Compare the integrals of one over x and one over x squared on the same infinite interval.
misconceptions.name: Every improper integral of a decaying integrand converges

misconceptions.description: The learner selects a technique from a visual resemblance to a worked example rather than from the structural precondition the technique requires.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to state the condition the chosen technique requires and to point to it in the integrand.
misconceptions.name: Technique choice follows the surface look of the integrand

misconceptions.description: The learner applies the theorem as a fixed template regardless of what the upper limit is.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the derivative of the upper limit on its own before the theorem is applied.
misconceptions.name: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus part one has no chain rule

misconceptions.description: The learner does not distinguish the bound variable inside the integral from the variable in the upper limit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether changing the letter of the variable of integration changes the function.
misconceptions.name: The variable of integration is the independent variable

misconceptions.description: The learner omits the interval or the units because the quantity has been identified.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what would change in the sentence if the interval were different.
misconceptions.name: An interpretation is complete once the quantity is named

misconceptions.description: The learner applies F(b) minus F(a) without checking that the integrand is continuous on the interval.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an integrand with a jump inside the interval and ask whether the theorem applies directly.
misconceptions.name: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus part two needs no hypotheses

misconceptions.description: The student takes the slope field to show one tangent line through the chosen point rather than a field of slopes to be followed, so the sketched solution is drawn straight or is replaced by a family of curves. The 2022 report names this as the most common misconception in that part.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the solution curve through a point on a field whose segments turn sharply; a student holding this belief draws a line or a curve that is too linear.
misconceptions.name: A slope field is a single tangent line at the point

misconceptions.description: The student treats the value of a convergent series as something approached by accumulating terms, so a partial sum is offered where a closed form was asked. The 2022 report records the behaviour and notes that in this course finding the value of a series calls on geometric series content; the belief itself is inferred from that pattern.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the exact value of a geometric series and then for a bound on the error of its third partial sum; a student holding this belief answers both with a decimal from partial sums.
misconceptions.name: A convergent series is evaluated by adding enough terms

misconceptions.description: The learner treats differentiation as an operation on the visible outer function, so whatever sits inside is copied across unchanged.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to differentiate the same outer function with a linear inside and with a quadratic inside and to compare the two answers.
misconceptions.name: Differentiation acts only on the outermost shell

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the chain rule as a product of two derivatives at one point, so the inner output plays no part in where the outer derivative is read.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a table in which the inner output is itself a listed input and ask where the outer derivative should be read.
misconceptions.name: The chain rule factors are evaluated at the same input

misconceptions.description: The learner treats dy/du times du/dx as a cancellation of symbols rather than as a statement about rates, so the notation carries the reasoning and the underlying composition is not seen.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to say what du/dx measures in the situation before any cancellation is written.
misconceptions.name: Leibniz notation is a fraction that cancels

misconceptions.description: The learner treats y as a second free variable rather than as a function of x, so differentiating a y term with respect to x produces no extra factor.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student what dy/dx would mean if y did not depend on x.
misconceptions.name: In an equation, y is an independent symbol

misconceptions.description: The learner reads a term containing both variables as one object rather than as a product, so the product rule never comes into view.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to name the two factors of the mixed term before differentiating it.
misconceptions.name: A short mixed term is a single symbol

misconceptions.description: The learner expects the implicit derivative to come out in x alone, so an expression containing y is read as unfinished and is manipulated until the y disappears.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student for the slope at two different points of the same curve with the same x coordinate.
misconceptions.name: dy/dx is a number rather than an expression in both variables

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the equation on dy/dx as the whole problem, so a value satisfying it is reported without checking that a point with that value lies on the curve.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to verify that the candidate point satisfies the original equation, as a separate step.
misconceptions.name: A tangent condition is a condition on dy/dx alone

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the input of the inverse and the input of the original function as the same number, so the matching pair is never located.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write the ordered pair on the original function that corresponds to the point on the inverse.
misconceptions.name: The inverse is evaluated wherever the original is

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the reciprocal formula as unconditional, so the requirement that the original derivative be nonzero is never checked or stated.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the tangent line to the inverse looks like at a point where the original curve has a horizontal tangent.
misconceptions.name: The inverse derivative rule has no hypotheses

misconceptions.description: The learner stores the three formulas as one family and selects among them by resemblance, so the radical and the rational forms are exchanged.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to say which of the three derivatives has a square root and why.
misconceptions.name: The inverse trigonometric formulas are interchangeable

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the three formulas as items to be memorised with no route back to the definition, so a forgotten formula leaves no recovery.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to start from the equation relating the sine of an angle to the variable and to recover the derivative.
misconceptions.name: An inverse trigonometric derivative cannot be derived

misconceptions.description: The learner selects a rule by the visual pattern of the expression rather than by the operation applied last, so nested structures are handled in the wrong order.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to state the last operation performed when the expression is evaluated at a number.
misconceptions.name: The differentiation rule follows from the look of the expression

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the second derivative as a separate construction rather than as the derivative of the first derivative, so the same rules are not reapplied.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to say what operation turns the first derivative into the second.
misconceptions.name: A higher derivative is a different kind of object

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the symbols for derivatives as labels attached to an answer rather than as operators with a meaning, so notation is mixed within a line without loss of sense to the writer.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to say aloud what the expression d/dx of y means and how it differs from dy/dx.
misconceptions.name: Derivative notation is decorative

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the limit as another name for evaluation, so a missing or displaced function value is read as a missing or displaced limit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a graph with an open circle at one height and a closed point at another over the same input and ask for the limit and the value separately.
misconceptions.name: The limit at a point is the value of the function there

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a single one sided approach as sufficient, so a jump is read as a limit equal to the value on whichever side was examined.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the left hand limit and the right hand limit as separate answers, then ask whether the two sided limit exists.
misconceptions.name: A limit exists whenever the function approaches something on one side

misconceptions.description: The learner expects the function to attain the limit value, so a function that approaches without attaining is read as having no limit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether a function can have a limit at an input where it is undefined, and ask for an example.
misconceptions.name: A limit is a prediction the function must eventually reach

misconceptions.description: The learner treats tabulated agreement as proof, so oscillation or behaviour between the tabulated inputs is not considered.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the function does at inputs between two adjacent rows of the table.
misconceptions.name: A table settles the behaviour of a function

misconceptions.description: The learner applies the quotient and composite theorems as formal rules without the denominator condition or the continuity condition on the outer function.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to state the condition each theorem requires and to point to where it was checked.
misconceptions.name: Limit theorems apply unconditionally

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the symbol zero over zero as an answer, reading it as zero, as undefined, or as a nonexistence verdict rather than as a signal to rewrite.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give two expressions with the same indeterminate form and different limits and ask for both values.
misconceptions.name: An indeterminate form is a value

misconceptions.description: The learner treats cancellation as a syntactic move on repeated symbols rather than a division of common factors, so terms are cancelled like factors.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to evaluate the original and the rewritten expression at one convenient input and compare.
misconceptions.name: Rewriting an expression may change any matching symbols

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the bounding functions as things to evaluate at the target rather than as functions whose limits must agree, and handles the inequality as an equation.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the bounding inequality must hold at the target input itself for the theorem to apply.
misconceptions.name: The squeeze theorem is a substitution rule

misconceptions.description: The learner holds one of the three conditions as the whole definition, most often that the function is defined there or that the one sided limits agree.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give one function defined at the point with unequal one sided limits and one whose limit exists but differs from the value, and ask about continuity in both.
misconceptions.name: Continuity is a single condition

misconceptions.description: The learner treats naming the definition or the theorem as the argument, so the values and conditions that make the claim true are never produced.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which feature of the given function or table makes the stated claim true.
misconceptions.name: Restating a definition counts as a justification

misconceptions.description: The learner reads any zero of the original denominator as unbounded behaviour without simplifying first.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the limit of the expression at that input after factoring numerator and denominator.
misconceptions.name: Every input missing from the domain is an asymptote

misconceptions.description: The learner treats an infinite limit as a two sided property and writes one statement where the two sides carry opposite signs, or reads the infinity symbol as a real value.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the sign of the quotient just to the left and just to the right of the input.
misconceptions.name: Unbounded behaviour is the same on both sides

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the infinity symbol as an input value, so end behaviour is computed by substitution and the conditions on degree comparison are skipped.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to divide numerator and denominator by the dominant power and to say what each resulting term approaches.
misconceptions.name: Infinity is a number that can be substituted

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a statement about the long run rate as a statement about the long run amount, so the wrong function is placed inside the limit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the units of the limit just written and compare them with the units the question asks about.
misconceptions.name: The end behaviour of a quantity and of its rate are interchangeable

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the stated setting as discharging the hypotheses of a theorem, so continuity is asserted rather than derived from a stated property.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what in the question establishes that the function is continuous on the interval.
misconceptions.name: A hypothesis is satisfied because the question implies it

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the conclusion of the Intermediate Value Theorem as producing a unique input, or applies it without checking that the target lies between the endpoint values.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the theorem rules out a second input with the same output and what it would take to find one.
misconceptions.name: An existence theorem locates or counts solutions

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the difference quotient over an interval as the rate at an instant, so no limiting process is invoked.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the average rate over two different intervals containing the same point and ask which one is the rate at that point.
misconceptions.name: An average rate over an interval is the rate at a point in it

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate a limit whose value is infinite from a limit taken as the variable grows without bound, so vertical and horizontal asymptote statements are exchanged.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to point to where the infinity symbol sits in each of two statements and to say what each claims.
misconceptions.name: All limit notation with an infinity symbol means the same thing

misconceptions.description: The learner reports a function as continuous everywhere because its formula belongs to a family continuous on its domain, without excluding the inputs outside that domain.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the inputs at which the expression is undefined before any interval is written.
misconceptions.name: Continuity is a property of a formula rather than of a domain

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate the list of terms from their accumulated total, so a statement about one is taken to settle the other.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give one general term and ask separately whether the sequence converges and whether the series converges.
misconceptions.name: A sequence and its series are the same object

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the total of the first few terms as the value of the infinite series, so no limit is taken.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the third and the fourth partial sums and whether both can be the value of the series.
misconceptions.name: A partial sum is the value of the series

misconceptions.description: The learner uses the closed form for a geometric sum whenever the terms decrease, without identifying a constant ratio or checking its size.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a p-series and ask for its common ratio.
misconceptions.name: The geometric sum formula applies to any series that shrinks

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the sum formula as requiring the term at index zero, regardless of where the series as written begins.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write the first two terms of a series whose sigma notation starts at index two.
misconceptions.name: The first term of a geometric series is always the index zero term

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the nth term test as a two way criterion, so a limit of zero is taken as proof of convergence.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the harmonic series does and whether its terms approach zero.
misconceptions.name: Terms approaching zero make a series converge

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the direction of a one way test as reversible, so failing the divergence condition is read as convergence.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what conclusion the nth term test permits when the limit is zero.
misconceptions.name: A test that establishes divergence also establishes convergence

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the name of a test as the argument, so the hypotheses are never verified and a test may be used on a series it does not cover.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to state the conditions of the chosen test and point to where each one holds.
misconceptions.name: A convergence test can be applied without checking its conditions

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the integral test as an evaluation rather than a comparison, so the integral's value is reported as the sum.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the first term of the series equals the area over the first subinterval.
misconceptions.name: The improper integral and the series have the same value

misconceptions.description: The learner remembers that some exponents give convergence but places the boundary elsewhere than at one, or applies the criterion to series that are not p-series.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the behaviour of the series with exponent one and with exponent two.
misconceptions.name: The p-series threshold is misplaced

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a comparison as an association between two similar series, so the direction of the term inequality is not tied to the conclusion drawn.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what follows when the terms are larger than those of a convergent series.
misconceptions.name: The comparison inequality works in either direction

misconceptions.description: The learner carries the ratio test habit into the limit comparison test and treats one as the deciding threshold rather than requiring a positive finite limit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the limit comparison test concludes when the limit is three.
misconceptions.name: The limit comparison value is compared with one

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the alternating factor as the whole of the test, so no condition on the sizes of the terms is checked.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an alternating series whose terms do not approach zero and ask whether it converges.
misconceptions.name: Alternating signs alone give convergence

misconceptions.description: The learner collapses the two requirements of the alternating series test into one statement, so only one of them is ever checked or stated.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for a sequence that decreases but does not approach zero.
misconceptions.name: Decreasing and tending to zero are a single condition

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a ratio limit of one as a result rather than as a failure of the test, and applies the ratio test where its limit gives nothing.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Apply the ratio test to the harmonic series and ask what it shows.
misconceptions.name: The ratio test settles every series

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the two words as interchangeable labels for a convergent series, so the test on the absolute value series is never separated from the test on the series itself.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the two tests was run and what the other one would show.
misconceptions.name: Absolute and conditional convergence are the same distinction

misconceptions.description: The learner orders the two classifications on a single scale, so a conditionally convergent series is taken to be absolutely convergent with a smaller margin, and rearrangement is assumed to be safe.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether rearranging the terms of the alternating harmonic series must leave its value unchanged.
misconceptions.name: Conditional convergence is a weaker form of absolute convergence

misconceptions.description: The learner treats an error bound as a formula attached to a partial sum, so neither the alternating series conditions nor the derivative bound is established first.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what has to be true of the series before the alternating series error bound may be used.
misconceptions.name: An error bound can be used without checking its conditions

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the bounding expression as the exact error, so the result is written with an equals sign and no comparison with a tolerance is made.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the approximation is off by exactly that amount or by at most that amount.
misconceptions.name: The bound is the error

misconceptions.description: The learner builds the polynomial by attaching derivative values directly to the powers, so the factorial denominators are absent or misassigned.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what coefficient a second derivative of six produces in the second degree term.
misconceptions.name: Taylor coefficients are the derivative values

misconceptions.description: The learner does not treat the requested degree as binding, so a polynomial is written with an ellipsis or a series is truncated without regard to the request.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask how many terms the requested object has and whether it ends.
misconceptions.name: A Taylor polynomial and a Taylor series are interchangeable

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the series representation as valid for all inputs, so the interval of convergence plays no part in statements about function values.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask at which inputs the series for one over one minus x gives the function value.
misconceptions.name: A function equals its Maclaurin series everywhere

misconceptions.description: The learner reports one when the other is requested, so an interval is offered as a radius or a radius is treated as a complete answer about convergence.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the radius and for the interval of the same series in turn.
misconceptions.name: Radius and interval of convergence are interchangeable

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the ratio test result as final, so the endpoints are never examined and the interval is reported open.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the ratio test says at an endpoint where the limit equals one.
misconceptions.name: The open interval from the ratio test is the interval of convergence

misconceptions.description: The learner tests one endpoint and transfers the verdict to the other, or applies the same test at both without checking that its conditions hold at each.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the series becomes at each endpoint and whether the two look alike.
misconceptions.name: The two endpoints behave the same way

misconceptions.description: The learner extends the preservation of the radius to the endpoints, so the interval of the original series is carried over unchanged.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the CED guarantees about a term-by-term derivative and what it does not.
misconceptions.name: A differentiated or integrated series inherits the whole interval

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a substitution as relocating the centre of the series, so the powers and the interval are adjusted as though the centre had moved.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the centre of the resulting series is after the substitution and what its powers are in.
misconceptions.name: Substituting into a known series changes where it is centred

misconceptions.description: The learner treats any request for an average as a single procedure and does not separate averaging the function values from averaging its rate of change.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the two answers carries the units of the function and which carries the units of a rate.
misconceptions.name: Average value and average rate of change are the same quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner sees the integral as the averaging operation itself, so the division by the length of the interval looks like an optional simplification.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the average value of the constant function two over an interval of length five.
misconceptions.name: The integral of a function is its average

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the integral expression as scratch work that supports the calculator rather than as the object being scored.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write, without the calculator, the expression whose value the calculator reported.
misconceptions.name: A calculator answer stands on its own

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the integral of velocity as the length of the trip, so the sign of the velocity plays no role.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a velocity that is positive on the first half of an interval and the negative of that on the second half, and ask for both quantities.
misconceptions.name: Distance travelled and net change in position are the same

misconceptions.description: The learner does not attach the absolute value to speed, so a negative speed is acceptable and the integrand for distance keeps its sign.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the speed of a particle whose velocity is a stated negative number.
misconceptions.name: Speed is another name for velocity

misconceptions.description: The learner reads an accumulation integral as the quantity itself rather than as the change in it, so the initial value has no role.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give one rate and two different starting amounts and ask for the value at the later time in each case.
misconceptions.name: The integral of a rate is the amount of the quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner attaches accumulation to every rate in the problem without attending to the direction in which each one moves the quantity.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the stored amount does at a time when the two rates are equal.
misconceptions.name: Two rates acting at once combine by addition

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the first or second derivative test as a complete justification, so the endpoints of the interval are never considered.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a function whose only interior critical point is a relative maximum but whose largest value on the interval is at an endpoint.
misconceptions.name: A local extremum argument settles an absolute extremum

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the sentence as a label for the integral rather than as a statement that must fix the quantity, the interval, and the units.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what would change in the sentence if the limits of the integral were different.
misconceptions.name: An interpretation is complete once the quantity is named

misconceptions.description: The learner treats area as always measured from the horizontal axis, so the second boundary curve is not subtracted.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the area between two horizontal lines and compare it with the integral of the upper line alone.
misconceptions.name: The area between curves is the integral of the curve that bounds it

misconceptions.description: The learner knows the area is positive and assumes any sign problem can be repaired at the end by taking the absolute value of the result.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write the statement that links the integral to the area and then to check it numerically.
misconceptions.name: The order of subtraction in an area integrand does not matter

misconceptions.description: The learner chooses limits from the axes of the picture or from the stated domain instead of from where the region actually begins and ends.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which inputs bound the shaded region and why those and not the ends of the axes.
misconceptions.name: Limits of integration are a viewing window rather than a boundary

misconceptions.description: The learner treats dx and dy as labels for the direction of slicing rather than as the variable the integrand must be written in.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to name every variable that appears in the integrand and compare it with the differential.
misconceptions.name: The differential can be changed without changing the integrand

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the area formula as a template applied once, so a crossing inside the interval does not signal that the region has pieces.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the sign of the integrand on each side of the interior crossing.
misconceptions.name: One integral covers any region between two curves

misconceptions.description: The learner associates pi with volume rather than with circular cross sections, so polygonal slices inherit it.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which shape the area formula inside the integral describes.
misconceptions.name: Every volume integral carries a factor of pi

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the slice as reaching from the axis to the curve even when the region is bounded by two curves.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to draw the slice on the figure and label both of its endpoints.
misconceptions.name: The cross sectional dimension is a function value

misconceptions.description: The learner treats squaring as distributing over subtraction, so a washer integrand is written with one squared difference.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to evaluate both expressions with the radii five and three.
misconceptions.name: The difference of squares equals the square of the difference

misconceptions.description: The learner substitutes the distance between the boundary curves into every circular formula without asking whether it is a radius or a diameter.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the radius of a semicircle whose diameter is a stated length.
misconceptions.name: The distance between the curves is always the radius

misconceptions.description: The learner remembers the squared dimension but not the fraction in front of it, so equilateral, triangular, and semicircular sections lose their constants.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the area of one slice of the named shape with a numerical dimension.
misconceptions.name: Area formulas are recalled without their constant factors

misconceptions.description: The learner carries the circle formula only as far as the factor pi, so the radius is not squared inside the integral.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the area of a single disc of a stated radius before the integral is written.
misconceptions.name: A volume of revolution integrates the radius rather than its square

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the disc and washer formulas as fixed in the function rather than as built from a distance to the axis.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the distance from a named point on the curve to the stated axis of revolution.
misconceptions.name: The radius is the function value whatever the axis of revolution is

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the translation as applying to the whole integral rather than to the radius alone.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which inputs the region occupies before the axis of revolution is named.
misconceptions.name: Moving the axis of revolution moves the limits of integration

misconceptions.description: The learner assigns the radii by position in the plane rather than by distance from the axis, which fails when the axis lies above the region.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Revolve the same region about a line above it and ask which curve is farther from that line.
misconceptions.name: The upper curve always gives the outer radius

misconceptions.description: The learner reads every definite integral as area under a graph, so a radical integrand is still described as an area and its own form is not examined.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what integrand would give the area under the same graph and compare it with the one displayed.
misconceptions.name: An integral over an interval measures an area

misconceptions.description: The learner treats an existence theorem as a rule that applies to any function, so the conditions never enter the written argument.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a function with a jump inside the interval and ask whether the conclusion still holds.
misconceptions.name: Hypotheses are decoration and the conclusion is the theorem

misconceptions.description: The learner believes that writing the name of the theorem completes the argument, so the verified hypothesis and the affirmative conclusion are left out.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which sentence of the response would convince a reader who had never heard of the theorem.
misconceptions.name: Naming a theorem is itself a justification

misconceptions.description: The learner averages the two outputs instead of dividing the change in output by the change in input.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the units of the quantity just computed and compare with the units of the derivative.
misconceptions.name: Average rate of change is the average of the endpoint values

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the conclusion as naming the input rather than asserting that one exists.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the theorem tells you about where the point is.
misconceptions.name: An existence theorem locates the point it asserts

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate a claim that the function takes a value from a claim that the derivative takes a value, so the Intermediate Value Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem are used interchangeably.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the two theorems concerns the derivative and which concerns the function.
misconceptions.name: One existence theorem serves for claims about values and about derivatives

misconceptions.description: The learner does not check the closed interval and applies the Extreme Value Theorem to open intervals or across discontinuities.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for a function on an open interval with no largest value.
misconceptions.name: Continuity may be assumed on any interval

misconceptions.description: The learner takes a local high or low point as the largest or smallest value on the whole interval.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether an endpoint can beat the interior candidate and how that is checked.
misconceptions.name: A relative extremum is an absolute extremum

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the derivative being zero as the definition of a turning point, so no sign change is checked.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for a function with a zero derivative at an input that is not an extremum.
misconceptions.name: Every critical point is an extremum

misconceptions.description: The learner does not look for corners, cusps, or vertical tangents, so that family of critical points never appears.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the derivative of the absolute value function at zero.
misconceptions.name: The derivative exists wherever the function does

misconceptions.description: The learner decides increase and decrease from whether the function values are positive or negative.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for a function that is negative everywhere and increasing everywhere.
misconceptions.name: The sign of the derivative follows the sign of the function

misconceptions.description: The learner answers questions about the function by reading features of whatever curve is drawn, even when the drawn curve is a derivative or an integrand.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to label the plotted curve and the function under discussion separately before answering.
misconceptions.name: The plotted curve is the function under discussion

misconceptions.description: The learner reports one interval of increase or concavity spanning an input where the function does not exist.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the domain of the function before any interval is reported.
misconceptions.name: A gap in the domain does not interrupt an interval of behaviour

misconceptions.description: The learner writes a second sentence that says the same thing in other symbols and believes the justification is complete.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what feature of the given graph makes the stated claim true.
misconceptions.name: Restating the conclusion counts as a reason

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the size or the sign of the derivative at one nearby input as the classification of the critical point.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the sign of the derivative on each side, in those words.
misconceptions.name: The classification comes from the derivative value rather than its change

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate the input at which the extremum occurs from the extreme value itself.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for both the input and the value and see which the student had reported.
misconceptions.name: The location of an extremum and its value are the same answer

misconceptions.description: The learner builds the candidate list from the interior critical points and does not regard the endpoints as competitors.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the function value at each end of the interval.
misconceptions.name: The candidates are the critical points only

misconceptions.description: The learner does not carry out the comparison and reports whichever candidate the work ended on.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the tabulated values is smallest and why.
misconceptions.name: The last candidate computed is the extremum

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a first or second derivative test as a proof that the extremum is the largest or smallest on the whole interval.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask how the candidate compares with the value at the far end of the interval.
misconceptions.name: A local test settles a global question

misconceptions.description: The learner transfers rules about the sign of the first derivative directly onto the second without re-deriving what they say.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what a positive second derivative says about the function and what it says about the first derivative.
misconceptions.name: The second derivative behaves like the first

misconceptions.description: The learner does not distinguish rising from bending upward, so the sign and the direction of the derivative are used interchangeably.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to sketch a decreasing concave up curve.
misconceptions.name: Concavity and monotonicity are the same property

misconceptions.description: The learner equates the candidate condition with the conclusion and never checks the sign change.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the second derivative does on each side of the disputed input.
misconceptions.name: A zero of the second derivative is a point of inflection

misconceptions.description: The learner supplies derivative notation in place of a statement about the object the question gave, and does not see the difference.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write the same reason without any derivative symbols.
misconceptions.name: A reason is complete once symbols appear

misconceptions.description: The learner does not hold the inconclusive case in mind and reads a zero second derivative as a verdict.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the test says when the second derivative is zero at the critical point.
misconceptions.name: The second derivative test always decides

misconceptions.description: The learner picks a test by habit rather than by what the given representation supports or what the question demands.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which derivative the given object shows and what the question is claiming.
misconceptions.name: The two derivative tests are interchangeable in every setting

misconceptions.description: The learner believes the derivative fixes one curve, so no value of the function is thought to be needed.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to name two different functions with the same given derivative.
misconceptions.name: A derivative determines its function uniquely

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a finite table of derivative values as a full description of the function.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether another function through the same table could behave differently between the entries.
misconceptions.name: A table of values settles behaviour between the listed inputs

misconceptions.description: The learner differentiates the first expression written down, whether it is the objective or the constraint, and reports its critical point.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which quantity the question wants made largest and which one is fixed.
misconceptions.name: An optimisation answer is the critical point of whatever expression appears first

misconceptions.description: The learner carries the algebraic domain of the reduced objective into the problem and ignores what the situation permits.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether a negative length would make sense in the situation.
misconceptions.name: The contextual domain is all inputs

misconceptions.description: The learner regards the vanishing derivative as the answer and sees no need for a verification step.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask how the student knows the critical point is a maximum rather than a minimum.
misconceptions.name: Finding a critical point finishes an optimisation

misconceptions.description: The learner reports the optimal number and regards the question as answered, with the quantity, the units, and the input left implicit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the number measures and when it is attained.
misconceptions.name: A numerical answer is a complete interpretation

misconceptions.description: The learner looks only at the numerator of the derivative expression and never at the denominator.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what happens to the tangent line where the denominator of the derivative vanishes.
misconceptions.name: A relation has critical points only where its derivative is zero

misconceptions.description: The learner treats an input value as a point, forgetting that a relation may pair it with several outputs or with none.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which outputs the relation pairs with the reported input.
misconceptions.name: A single coordinate names a point on a relation

misconceptions.description: The learner differentiates expressions in the second variable without the chain rule, and leaves the derivative symbol unsubstituted.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the derivative of the square of the dependent variable with respect to the independent one.
misconceptions.name: Implicit differentiation may treat the dependent variable as a constant

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the change in the quantity as the rate itself, so the division by the change in the input is omitted or applied to the wrong pair of values.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the units of the reported number and compare them with the units the question asks for.
misconceptions.name: A rate is a difference

misconceptions.description: The learner regards the limit definition as a ritual line, so the increment is set to zero immediately or the answer is produced by a rule and the definition is copied around it.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to point to the step in the work where the increment stops appearing in the denominator, and why it may be removed there.
misconceptions.name: The definition of the derivative is a formality to be written and then abandoned

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the limit as attaching to the answer rather than to every expression in the chain, so intermediate lines assert equalities that are false before the limit is taken.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to read the second line of the work as a sentence and say whether it is true for every increment.
misconceptions.name: The limit symbol is decoration on the final line

misconceptions.description: The learner treats every indeterminate limit as an algebra problem, so a difference quotient whose underlying derivative is known is not recognised as such.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to name a function whose values appear in the numerator and what input it is evaluated at.
misconceptions.name: A limit is resolved only by algebra

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the stated context as discharging a hypothesis, so continuity is asserted rather than derived from the differentiability stated in the stem.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what in the question establishes that the function is continuous.
misconceptions.name: A hypothesis holds because the setting supplies it

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the implication as running in both directions, so continuity at a point is taken to supply a derivative there.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for a function continuous at a point at which it has no derivative, and then for one differentiable but not continuous there.
misconceptions.name: Differentiability and continuity are the same property

misconceptions.description: The learner decides whether a derivative exists from how the curve looks rather than from the one sided behaviour of the difference quotient, so a vertical tangent is read as a slope and a smooth looking point is assumed differentiable.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the slope approached from each side as two separate numbers before the verdict is given.
misconceptions.name: Differentiability is a visual property of the graph

misconceptions.description: The learner treats units as optional, or copies them from the table header, so the compound units of a rate are not produced.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the denominator of the quotient measures and what the resulting compound unit is.
misconceptions.name: Units are decoration rather than part of the answer

misconceptions.description: The learner remembers the exponent decreasing but not the multiplication by the original exponent, and does not see constants and radicals as powers.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to differentiate a squared term from the definition and compare the result with the rule.
misconceptions.name: The power rule is a move on the exponent alone

misconceptions.description: The learner applies the exponent move to transcendental functions, so the natural exponential is treated as a power and the trigonometric signs are not carried.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the base and the exponent contains the variable in the expression being differentiated.
misconceptions.name: Every function is differentiated by the power rule

misconceptions.description: The learner extends the term by term rule to products, so the derivative of a product is taken as the product of the derivatives and supplied values are placed in the wrong positions.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to expand a simple product, differentiate term by term, and compare with the proposed answer.
misconceptions.name: Differentiation distributes across a product

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the two numerator terms as interchangeable and the denominator as carrying no square, so sign and structure errors follow.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to apply the rule to a reciprocal whose derivative the power rule already gives and compare the two results.
misconceptions.name: The quotient rule is symmetric

misconceptions.description: The learner memorises the four derivatives without the rewriting that produces them, so signs and cofunction pairings are exchanged and no recovery route is available.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to obtain the derivative from the sine and cosine form rather than from memory.
misconceptions.name: The remaining trigonometric derivatives are independent facts

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the two numbers computed at the point of tangency as playing the same role, so the height is used as a slope or the slope as a height.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the two computed numbers has the units of a slope.
misconceptions.name: The derivative and the function value are interchangeable at a point

misconceptions.description: The learner does not read the notation as naming a function, an independent variable, and possibly a point of evaluation, so the Leibniz form is treated as a fraction and the derivative function is confused with its value.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the symbol denotes and whether the object it names depends on the variable.
misconceptions.name: Derivative notation is a set of interchangeable labels

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a contextual question as asking about the modelled quantity regardless of whether the question concerns its amount or its rate of change.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give the value of the function and the value of its derivative at the same input and ask which one answers the question and why.
misconceptions.name: The derivative and the quantity are the same information

misconceptions.description: The learner reports the magnitude of a rate and treats its sign as a formatting detail rather than as the statement that the quantity is falling.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the quantity was larger or smaller a moment after the instant described.
misconceptions.name: The sign of a rate is decoration

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the unit as something added at the end if time allows rather than as part of what the derivative is.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the units of the answer before the computation is done, from the units in the stem alone.
misconceptions.name: Units are an ornament on the answer

misconceptions.description: The learner stores the three motion functions as separate items rather than as one function and its successive derivatives, so which one to differentiate is decided by guesswork.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the three the stem supplied and what operation reaches each of the other two.
misconceptions.name: Position, velocity, and acceleration are three unrelated formulas

misconceptions.description: The learner uses the two words interchangeably, so the sign that records direction is either lost or is reported as part of a speed.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a negative velocity and ask separately for the speed and for the direction of motion.
misconceptions.name: Speed and velocity are the same quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner reads positive acceleration as speeding up, treating the sign of the velocity as irrelevant to the question.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give negative velocity with positive acceleration and ask whether the particle is speeding up.
misconceptions.name: Acceleration alone settles whether speed is increasing

misconceptions.description: The learner maps every rate context onto the vocabulary of a moving particle, so the quantity in the situation is described as a position or a velocity.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to name the quantity and its units and then to reread their own sentence.
misconceptions.name: Rate problems are motion problems

misconceptions.description: The learner carries the habit of differentiating with respect to x into a time based problem, so the rates with respect to time never appear.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what variable the requested rate is taken with respect to and which letters in the equation depend on it.
misconceptions.name: Differentiating a relation means differentiating with respect to a length

misconceptions.description: The learner reads a term that multiplies two changing quantities as one object, so only one rate factor appears where two are needed.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to name the two factors of the term and to say whether each one changes with time.
misconceptions.name: A short product is a single varying symbol

misconceptions.description: The learner expects the supplied rates to determine the answer without a geometric relation, so the equation is skipped or is chosen by resemblance.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to draw the configuration and to say which formula describes it.
misconceptions.name: The relating equation can be assembled from the rates alone

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the measurements given for the instant in question as fixed features of the configuration, so they are substituted before the differentiation.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the stated numbers would still hold one second later, before any differentiation.
misconceptions.name: A value true at an instant is true throughout

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the tangent line value as the function value rather than as an approximation, so the distinction between the two inputs and the question of error direction do not arise.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask how far the tangent line value is from the function value and which of the two is larger.
misconceptions.name: The tangent line is the function near the point

misconceptions.description: The learner settles whether the tangent line is above or below the curve from the sign of the first derivative rather than from the concavity.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an increasing concave down function and ask for the direction of the tangent line error, then repeat with an increasing concave up function.
misconceptions.name: The direction of the approximation error follows from increase or decrease

misconceptions.description: The learner treats zero over zero and infinity over infinity as values that may be written on the right of an equals sign and manipulated.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to say what the symbol on the right of their equals sign names.
misconceptions.name: Indeterminate forms are numbers

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the rule as a general device for limits that resist substitution, so no form is checked before it is used.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a limit of a quotient that is not indeterminate and ask whether the rule may be applied.
misconceptions.name: L'Hospital's rule applies to any awkward limit

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the conclusion as the limit of the derivative of the quotient rather than as the limit of the quotient of the derivatives.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write the numerator derivative and the denominator derivative on separate lines before assembling anything.
misconceptions.name: The rule differentiates the quotient

misconceptions.description: The learner treats values computed at a few inputs as settling the sign of a function across the whole interval, so zeros between samples are missed and the communicated conclusion does not cover the interval.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a velocity with a non-integer zero and ask for the intervals on which it is negative.
misconceptions.name: Sampled values establish behaviour on an interval

misconceptions.description: The learner treats t as if it were x, so derivatives with respect to the parameter are read as slopes and points on the curve are confused with parameter values.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the coordinates of the point at a stated parameter value and then for the slope there.
misconceptions.name: The parameter is the horizontal coordinate

misconceptions.description: The learner carries the single variable habit that the derivative of the vertical quantity is the slope, so the horizontal rate never enters.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a path whose horizontal rate is two and ask for both dy/dt and the slope.
misconceptions.name: The slope of a parametric path is the rate of the vertical component

misconceptions.description: The learner remembers that a quotient of the two component rates gives the slope but not which is the numerator, so the reciprocal looks equally acceptable.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the slope should be on a path where the horizontal rate is large and the vertical rate is small.
misconceptions.name: The order of the parametric quotient does not matter

misconceptions.description: The learner generalises the quotient rule for dy/dx by replacing each first derivative with a second derivative, so the intermediate differentiation of the slope disappears.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which function is being differentiated at the second step and with respect to which variable.
misconceptions.name: The second derivative follows the same pattern as the first

misconceptions.description: The learner adds the horizontal and vertical rates rather than combining them by the Pythagorean relation.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the speed of a particle with component rates three and four.
misconceptions.name: A length in the plane is the sum of the two component contributions

misconceptions.description: The learner integrates the velocity components and takes a magnitude at the end, so a path that doubles back is measured as if it were straight.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for both quantities for a particle that returns to its starting point.
misconceptions.name: Distance travelled in the plane is the size of the net change in position

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the limits as a window that merely has to include the object, so an interval that retraces part of the curve looks harmless.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask at which parameter values the curve revisits a point it has already passed.
misconceptions.name: Any interval containing the curve gives its length or area

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the written expression as scratch work supporting the calculator rather than as the object being scored.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write the expression the calculator evaluated, without using the calculator.
misconceptions.name: A calculator result stands without its expression

misconceptions.description: The learner reports two values without treating them as components of one object, so labels, order, and a single constant of integration all look immaterial.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the two reported numbers is the horizontal component and why.
misconceptions.name: A vector answer is a pair of numbers with no structure

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the accumulation as the position itself rather than as the change in it, so the known position plays no role.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the same coordinate with the known position moved to a different point.
misconceptions.name: The integral of a velocity component is the coordinate

misconceptions.description: The learner reports the larger component, or one chosen component, as the speed, so the magnitude never appears.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the speed at a time when one component is zero and the other is not.
misconceptions.name: Speed is one of the two velocity components

misconceptions.description: The learner reads approach to an axis from where the coordinate is small or negative rather than from the sign of its rate.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the rate is doing at a time when the coordinate is positive and the particle is approaching the axis.
misconceptions.name: The direction of motion is given by the sign of the position
