misconceptions.description: The learner treats r as a coordinate of the point, so the conversion by cosine and sine is skipped.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for both Cartesian coordinates of the point at a stated angle on the curve.
misconceptions.name: The polar radius is a Cartesian coordinate

misconceptions.description: The learner attaches every derivative to motion along the path, so the rate at which the distance from the origin changes is read as a speed and the rate of the angle is left out.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what quantity r measures, and then what the units of the requested rate are.
misconceptions.name: The derivative of r is the speed along the curve

misconceptions.description: The learner transfers the single variable pattern that the derivative of the given function is the slope, so the conversion to Cartesian coordinates never happens.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the slope of the tangent to a circle of constant radius, where dr/dtheta is zero everywhere.
misconceptions.name: The slope of a polar curve is the derivative of r

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a derivative test as a complete justification, so the endpoints of the angle interval are never compared.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the value of the coordinate at both ends of the angle interval.
misconceptions.name: A local extremum argument settles a farthest point

misconceptions.description: The learner transports the Cartesian area formula unchanged, so neither the square of r nor the factor of one half appears.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the area of a circular sector of stated radius and angle, then compare with the integral written.
misconceptions.name: A polar area is an integral of the curve itself

misconceptions.description: The learner subtracts the radii before squaring, treating the ring as a single sector of the difference.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to evaluate both expressions with the radii two and one.
misconceptions.name: The area between polar curves uses the difference of the radii

misconceptions.description: The learner takes the angle range in which the picture is drawn as the limits instead of the angles where the curves meet.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask at which angles the two curves meet before any integral is written.
misconceptions.name: The limits of a polar area are the whole interval of the figure

misconceptions.description: The learner drops the constant of proportionality, so the modelled rate is set equal to the quantity or to the difference itself.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask where the constant of proportionality went.
misconceptions.name: Proportional to means equal to

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate a constraint on the rate from a formula for the amount.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the left side of the written equation measures.
misconceptions.name: A differential equation is an equation for the quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the stated value as a term of the equation rather than as the condition that selects one solution.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which sentence of the problem would change if the starting value were different.
misconceptions.name: An initial condition is part of the differential equation

misconceptions.description: The learner accepts a candidate whose shape resembles what the equation suggests, without differentiating and substituting.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to differentiate the candidate and compare both sides.
misconceptions.name: A plausible looking function is a solution

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the equation as determining a single function, so the family and the constant have no role.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to name two different functions that satisfy the same equation.
misconceptions.name: A differential equation has one solution

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the segments as points of a curve rather than as directions, so the field is treated as a plot.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the tilt of one segment represents.
misconceptions.name: A slope field shows values of the solution

misconceptions.description: The learner reads a zero slope as a turning point rather than as a possible equilibrium.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the constant function at that level does in the equation.
misconceptions.name: A horizontal segment marks a maximum of every solution

misconceptions.description: The learner draws a smooth curve through the initial point without keeping it tangent to the segments.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the drawn curve is tangent to the segment at each point it passes.
misconceptions.name: A solution curve may be drawn freely through the field

misconceptions.description: The learner does not see the constant function at the level of zero slope as itself a solution that other solutions cannot cross.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the rate of change is exactly at that level.
misconceptions.name: A solution may cross an equilibrium level

misconceptions.description: The learner decides whether an estimate is high or low from the monotonicity of the solution rather than from its concavity.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an increasing concave down solution and ask for the direction of a tangent line estimate.
misconceptions.name: The direction of an approximation follows from increase or decrease

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the procedure as a single tangent line extended over the whole interval.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which point the slope is evaluated at on the second step.
misconceptions.name: Euler's method evaluates the derivative once

misconceptions.description: The learner advances the input but not the output, so every step uses the original point.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the input and the output used at the start of the second step.
misconceptions.name: Each Euler step restarts from the initial value

misconceptions.description: The learner regards the numerical result as the response, so the procedure is done mentally or on scratch paper.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to label the columns of their own table.
misconceptions.name: An answer needs no visible steps

misconceptions.description: The learner applies the separation move to every equation, whether or not the right side factors.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an equation whose right side is a sum in both variables and ask for the separated form.
misconceptions.name: Any differential equation can be separated

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the separation as a rearrangement and integrates only the side that looks like the target.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what happened to the differential on the other side.
misconceptions.name: Antidifferentiating one side is enough

misconceptions.description: The learner antidifferentiates without a constant, so the family collapses and the initial condition has nothing to act on.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the answer would be if the starting value were doubled.
misconceptions.name: The constant of integration is optional

misconceptions.description: The learner stops at an equation relating the two variables when an explicit expression was asked for.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the value of the dependent variable at a stated input.
misconceptions.name: An implicit relation is a finished solution

misconceptions.description: The learner removes an absolute value by habit, with no appeal to the initial condition or a stated bound.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the enclosed expression is positive or negative at the initial point.
misconceptions.name: An absolute value can be dropped without checking

misconceptions.description: The learner reports the algebraic expression with no regard for where it is defined or which branch contains the initial point.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what happens to the formula at the input where its denominator vanishes.
misconceptions.name: A solution formula holds on every input

misconceptions.description: The learner does not recognise the initial value plus a definite integral as a complete particular solution.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the initial value plus an integral satisfies the equation and the initial condition.
misconceptions.name: A particular solution must be written in closed form

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a constant rate constant as a constant rate, so the model comes out linear.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the solution looks like when the rate doubles as the amount doubles.
misconceptions.name: Proportional growth is linear growth

misconceptions.description: The learner does not see that the initial value fixes the leading coefficient and a second pair is needed for the exponent.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which two pieces of data the constant needs.
misconceptions.name: The constant of proportionality can be read off one data pair

misconceptions.description: The learner reports the number and leaves the quantity, the units, and the direction implicit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the number measures and in what units.
misconceptions.name: A numerical answer is a complete interpretation

misconceptions.description: The learner writes or reads the logistic equation without the factor that makes the rate vanish at the carrying capacity.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what happens to the rate when the quantity reaches the carrying capacity.
misconceptions.name: The logistic model is the exponential model with a harmless extra factor

misconceptions.description: The learner does not read the capacity off the zeros of the right side and reaches for partial fractions instead.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what value of the quantity makes the rate zero.
misconceptions.name: The carrying capacity must be found by solving the equation

misconceptions.description: The learner believes nothing can be said about long-run behaviour until the equation is solved, although the sign of the rate settles it.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which values of the quantity make the rate positive and which make it negative.
misconceptions.name: The limit of a solution needs the solution formula

misconceptions.description: The learner equates the largest value of the quantity with the largest value of its rate.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the rate exactly at the carrying capacity.
misconceptions.name: The quantity changes fastest at the carrying capacity
